prompt: Match each of the lesson's three questions to the Faro number it questions.

pairs.right: The driver's scan that says a box was late
The exit survey that blames price
The on-time rate Ligeiro is paid a bonus on

prompt: Drivers batch their scans the next morning. What happens to Marina's data?

choices.text: Nothing, because the scan is made at the door of the customer every time
choices.why: That is the question, not a given.

choices.text: The late share goes down, since batching makes every delivery look faster
choices.why: Batching later can only make deliveries look later.

choices.text: Some on-time boxes look late
choices.why: A delivery made on time and scanned the next day crosses the promised date in the data.

choices.text: The data is deleted
choices.why: No.

prompt: Why trace twenty first orders by hand, by the lesson?

choices.text: To measure the late rate more precisely than the scan data could
choices.why: Twenty records cannot prove a rate.

choices.text: Because finance requires a manual audit of every analysis that is presented
choices.why: No such requirement.

choices.text: To replace the carrier's data with a sample of customer messages
choices.why: It checks the data; it does not replace it.

choices.text: To expose a misread definition
choices.why: A handful of records reveals what a field really means.

prompt: Whether a measure measures what it claims to is called its ___.
How many of the 1,320 early cancellers answered the exit survey?
The survey puts price first and delivery third. Why does Marina still weigh delivery more?

choices.text: The cancellation rates are behaviour measured on all 6,113; the survey is the 23% who chose to answer
choices.why: Behaviour on the whole group outweighs stated reasons from a self-selected part.

choices.text: Surveys are always wrong
choices.why: It is still a clue to other causes.

choices.text: Price cannot be changed
choices.why: Not the argument.

choices.text: Because delivery is easier to fix
choices.why: Ease does not decide what is true.

prompt: Why might "too expensive" be over-represented in exit-survey answers?

choices.text: Because Faro's price is higher than every competitor's
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: It is a polite reason that needs no story
choices.why: A late box weeks earlier may not be what a customer names, even if it started the search.

choices.text: Price is the last option
choices.why: It is the first option listed.

choices.text: It is true for most
choices.why: Nobody knows for most; 77% did not answer.

prompt: Faro analyses only customers still subscribed after a year. What would it likely conclude about first deliveries?

choices.text: That first deliveries matter more than any other factor in the business
choices.why: The customers it drove away would be missing.

choices.text: That late first deliveries are a problem only in the interior of the state
choices.why: Not what survivorship produces.

choices.text: That the sample is too large to analyse in a spreadsheet tool
choices.why: Size is not the issue.

choices.text: That they barely matter
choices.why: The people they drove away are no longer in the data; cohorts avoid this.

prompt: Which statement is Strathern's form of Goodhart's law?

choices.text: What gets measured gets managed, and what is managed gets better over time
choices.why: A management slogan, and roughly the opposite warning.

choices.text: Numbers never lie, but the people who report them sometimes do
choices.why: Not the law, and it blames people rather than the incentive.

choices.text: A measure that becomes a target stops being good
choices.why: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

choices.text: Correlation is not causation
choices.why: True, and a different idea.

prompt: To one decimal place, what share of first boxes would count as on time under a three-day promise?
hint: Add days one, two and three.

prompt: Ligeiro is paid a bonus on its on-time rate. What does the lesson say to do with that fact?

choices.text: Use it as the reason to check the definition Ligeiro controls
choices.why: An incentive tells you where to look first, not what you will find.

choices.text: Accuse Ligeiro of gaming
choices.why: Nothing has been shown, and accusation poisons the conversation.

choices.text: Ignore it
choices.why: It is where to look first.

choices.text: Cancel the bonus
choices.why: Not the analyst's decision, nor the lesson's advice.

prompt: What defence against an incentive does the lesson give?
hint: A measure nobody is paid on.

choices.text: Removing every bonus that is tied to a measure the analyst uses
choices.why: Not the analyst's call, and not the advice.

choices.text: Read a second measure the incentive does not touch
choices.why: Customer-service tickets about late first boxes, beside the carrier's scans.

choices.text: Trusting only internal data
choices.why: Internal teams have incentives too.

choices.text: Asking Ligeiro
choices.why: Not a defence.

prompt: How does confirmation bias show up in an analyst, by the lesson?

choices.text: As a deliberate decision to hide the results that disagree with the finding
choices.why: It needs no dishonesty; it works quietly on careful people.

choices.text: As a preference for charts over tables in a presentation to the board
choices.why: Not related.

choices.text: A disappointing check run twice
choices.why: And a pleasing one run once.

choices.text: As using too few decimals
choices.why: No.

prompt: Why write down what would change your mind before looking?

choices.text: Because the board asks to see that list before approving any analysis
choices.why: No such request.

choices.text: So that the analysis takes longer and is therefore seen as more careful
choices.why: Time is not care.

choices.text: Because it makes the presentation one slide longer and so more complete
choices.why: Not the point.

choices.text: So it cannot be quietly revised
choices.why: Written in advance, the test cannot move after the result.

prompt: Which habits does the lesson give against your own bias? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Write what would change your mind before looking
choices.why: It cannot be revised after the result.

choices.text: Look for the evidence against you on purpose
choices.why: Ask what you would see if you were wrong.

choices.text: Let somebody else try to break it
choices.why: The red team of lesson 10.

choices.text: Run each check until it gives the result you expected
choices.why: That is the bias itself.

prompt: Which result in Marina's own analysis does the lesson cite as resisting her bias?
hint: The half she would not have chosen.

choices.why: That is the finding itself.

choices.text: Reporting that region explains a small part of the pooled gap
choices.why: She ran a test that could shrink her finding and reported what it found.

choices.text: The R$ 790 thousand
choices.why: A translation of the finding, not a test of it.

choices.text: The pilot target
choices.why: A decision, not a result.

prompt: When should you raise a checklist question about a colleague's number in a meeting?

choices.text: Only when the answer would change what the room decides
choices.why: Everything else goes to the colleague privately, as a question.

choices.text: Always
choices.why: That makes enemies and helps nobody.

choices.text: Never
choices.why: The one that changes the decision should be asked.

choices.text: At the end
choices.why: Timing is not the rule.

prompt: Put these checklist questions in the order the lesson's table gives them.
hint: Definition first, your own bias last.
items: Who benefits if it says this?

prompt: A row of the checklist you cannot answer for your own analysis is what, by the lesson?

choices.text: A sign the analysis should be abandoned and started again from scratch
choices.why: Too drastic; most gaps can be closed or stated.

choices.text: Something to hide until somebody asks about it in the meeting
choices.why: That is how a caveat costs trust.

choices.text: A gap to close, or a caveat to state
choices.why: Either before presenting, or out loud when you do.

choices.text: Irrelevant
choices.why: Every row catches something.

prompt: Late first deliveries suddenly fall to 5% in one week with no change in the warehouse. Which question comes first?
hint: A change in the number without a change in the work.

choices.text: Whether to celebrate the result with the team before the next quarterly review
choices.why: Not before knowing why it moved.

choices.text: Whether the board should be told at once, so that it can update its targets
choices.why: Too early.

choices.text: Whether the pilot can now be extended to the capital as originally planned
choices.why: Nothing changed in the work.

choices.text: Did the definition or the scan change?
choices.why: A number that moves without the work moving points at the source or the incentive first.
